claims.text: Adding approximately 5 atomic% Ag during melting or alloying is the proposed intervention.
Ag addition will produce a self-lubricating high-entropy-alloy composite.
Ag addition will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate.
The reduction in friction and wear will persist from ambient temperature to approximately 600°C.
Added Ag will form nanoprecipitates or segregated grain-boundary layers.
Mechanical stress during sliding will transform or redistribute the Ag-rich features into a continuous, low-shear-strength tribolayer.
Ag segregates to the sliding interface during operation.
Soft, ductile Ag accommodates shear stresses and reduces local stress concentrations.
The Ag-rich tribolayer and associated stress accommodation lower friction and wear.
Approximately 5 atomic% Ag will reduce coefficient of friction by about 30–50% relative to the undoped alloy.
Approximately 5 atomic% Ag will reduce wear rate by about 30–50% relative to the undoped alloy.
A sufficiently high service temperature is required to facilitate beneficial Ag segregation.
Excessive Ag migration or alloy destabilization can eliminate the intervention's effectiveness.
Extreme thermal cycling can compromise the effectiveness of Ag addition.
Overly oxidizing environments can cause Ag depletion and compromise effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts maintained effectiveness from ambient temperature to about 600°C, but the boundary states that service temperature must be high enough to facilitate Ag segregation. It does not establish that ambient temperature satisfies this requirement.

The predicted outcome is a 30–50% reduction maintained across the service-temperature range, whereas the falsification rule focuses on reductions below 20% at a majority of temperature points. Results between 20% and 30%, or failure at a minority of temperatures, could violate the stated prediction without falsifying it.
